Librarians' adoption and use of Koha Automation software in selected academic Libraries 
in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania 
Consolatha Joseph Mallya 
M A (Information Studies) 
University of Dar es Salaam, College of Social Science, 2019 
 
This study assessed librarians' adoption and use of Koha automation software in selected 
academic libraries in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. The study examined functional use of KOHA, 
librarian‘s skills and competences levels in using KOHA, evaluated librarians‘ satisfaction with 
KOHA, identified and analysed hurdles faced by librarians when using KOHA and finally 
proposed measures to resolve the problems. The study adopted a descriptive case study design 
and involved the Open University of Tanzania (OUT), Institute of Finance Management (IFM), 
and the College of Business Education (CBE) as purposefully sampled cases to represent the 
population of academic libraries which implement the KOHA software in Dar es Salaam region 
in Tanzania. Mixed methods approaches were employed to collect data for the research.

With the increasing number of students, workers and the community 
needs, SAUT expanded library and library services, The five-storey 
Archbishop Mario Mgulunde Learning Resource Centre building started 
to offer library services from the time it was blessed on the graduation 
day, 25"' November 2007 and opened for use on the 2' of January 2008. It 
is now doing a good job in the provision of library services. With space for 
a telecommunications centre at its very top, the library has space enough 
to hold thousands of books with many computers installed, accessible 
internet and various data base. ' Books are already available for use. 
Currently, according to the library report SAUT has 73,286 hard copies 
of books and lots of electronic resources such as books, journals and 
articles, There are 69 computers in the library. This is however, very far 
from the computer number required in the library serving more than 
thirteen thousand people. As for 2023, the ratio was one computer for 
1,062 students. Here, the number of the staff and the community around 
are not considered. There is therefore a need to increase computers in the 
library. The internet is also available to make sure the library offers the best 
services to both students and the staff. Unreliable internet connectivity 
due to insufficient bandwidth and unreliable power supply affecting the 
utilization of electronic resources are among bigger challenges to library 
users 
Library services are by both card catalogue and an online catalogue. The 
library capacity is to accommodate 1,500 people (students, workers etc.) 
at one sitting. There is a need for a fully functioning modern catalogue of 
library holdings. Encouraging and motivating students and the community 
to make fully use of library is another challenge awaiting the University 
to act on. There is a need also to encourage departmental, faculty or any 
other mini-libraries to be put in place for effectiveness of library use.

3.3.3 St. Augustine University of Tanzania Library 
St. Augustine University of Tanzania (SAUT), a religious and private institution of 
higher learning owned and managed by the Catholic Church, is dedicated to St. 
Augustine of Hippo (345-430 A.D). Its Motto is “Building the City of God.” SAUT was 
established in 1998 when it became a fully-fledged university. Before then, it was 
known as Nyegezi Social Training Institute (NSTI) established in 1960 by the Catholic 
White Fathers. In the early sixties, the White Fathers realised that skills in 
communication, community development, accounting, management and administration 
needed to be developed to prepare leaders who would take up positions in the emerging 
independent African countries, including Tanzania (SAUT, 2015). 
The mission of the Archbishop Mgulunde Resource Centre located at the Malimbe site is 
to support academic activities of teaching, learning and research. The learning centre 
plays a central role in promoting academic excellence. It is an organic combination of 
people, collection and facilities, whose purpose is to help users in the process of 
transforming information into knowledge. Information and knowledge are central to the 
attainment of the university’s mission and vision. 
The university library has thousands of volumes, which cover subject areas taught at 
SAUT, acquired though purchases, donations and gifts. The library also subscribes to 
several printed and e-journals databases. The library users can also access other 
databases through the internet in the library. The library has an online public catalogue

In Uganda, the use of FOSLMS has gained momentum. Many libraries including those in HEIs 
are turning to FOSLMS. In Uganda, Koha has stolen the show too, with many libraries adopting 
it. According to Adoma and Ponelis (2015), Koha is by far the most recognised open source 
integrated library system. This prompted the Consortium of Uganda University Libraries (CUUL) 
to recommend and encourage the adoption of Koha in all Ugandan libraries and arranged training 
for its membership in 2011. As a result, many libraries in HEIs in Uganda use Koha. These include, 
Uganda Christian University Library and Kyambogo University Library (Marshall Breeding, 
2018; Buwule & Ponelis, 2015). Below are some of the HEIs that have adopted Koha in Uganda.

among HEIs is widespread and Koha has more adoption footprints. Further, it has emerged that 
both private and public HEIs have adopted them.  This is contrary to the findings on Ethiopia in 
which only public HEIs are documented on the adoption of FOSLMS. 
Tanzania is also another country in East Africa that have adopted s FOSLMS. In the library sector,

## Abstract

This study examines the adoption and implementation of Free and Open Source Software (FOSS), particularly Koha, within libraries in Tanzania. Through assessing the perceptions and experiences of Library and Information Science (LIS) professionals regarding Koha's development and use, the research aims to identify the challenges and opportunities for improving library services in the country. Factors influencing the slow uptake of FOSS in Tanzanian libraries, such as inadequate staff training and lack of managerial support, are discussed, alongside broader implications for enhancing library automation and service provision.
